title: Regulatory Frameworks for Commemorative Performance: The Challenge of Transient Memory
text:
The existence and global rise of performance art utilized in cultural commemoration exposes significant regulatory lacunae concerning intellectual property and public space governance. Existing copyright law is fundamentally rooted in the premise of authorship, fixity, and permanence—principles incompatible with ephemeral, communal acts of memory. This framework struggles to protect intangible collective histories embedded solely within a time-bound physical gathering; once the performance concludes, the work ceases to legally exist for traditional enforcement purposes.

Furthermore, municipal ordinances governing public assembly are typically structured around minimizing disruption or controlling commercialization, rather than accommodating deep cultural significance. This creates an inadequate policy gap when communities require temporary, non-commercial exemptions in shared spaces to enact rituals of remembrance. Current regulations fail to adequately distinguish between disruptive street activity and vital acts of symbolic collective commemoration.

The urgent necessity lies in developing legal instruments that acknowledge 'Communal Ephemeral Rights'—a novel category recognizing the inherent value of organized cultural transience. Such a framework would need to allow for temporary, contextual governmental recognition of performance events not as activities requiring mitigation, but as legally protected mechanisms for cultural memory and social reproduction.
